Iran in the Post-War WorldSadegh Al-HosseiniThe aggressor side was defeated and failed to achieve any of its declared objectives, and the "four-to-six-week" war dragged on for seven months. But this victory has not brought peace. The Strait has remained open at a heavy cost to America, yet diesel has become America's Achilles' heel on America's doorstep. On the other hand, with Iran's exports reduced to zero, closing Hormuz has become less costly for Iran.Iran and America are trapped in a Nash equilibrium in which whichever side backs down first is the loser. The period from 12 Aban to 13 Dey is the most dangerous.Year-on-year inflation stands at around 83%, two-year cumulative growth is around negative 12%, and oil exports are near zero. Roughly 25 million people live below the poverty line, 15 million of whom are the newly poor.Time is not working in Iran's favor. Iran's trump card is lowering the cost of standing firm by improving the economy and opening up the political space, and this opportunity shrinks with each passing month. But with the figures and numbers presented in this report, if domestic politics and the economy are managed properly, Iran will emerge in the post-war world in a very powerful position.To read the 40-page article "Iran After the War," download the PDF file.

A hundred years of Iran's economy, in one chart. Six times in this hundred years, both employment fell and prices rose. It's called stagflation — the worst disease an economy can catch, because the cure for each one is the other's pain. 1320: occupation. 1367: the year the war ended. 1373: foreign debt crisis. 1391: sanctions. 1397: Trump's withdrawal from the JCPOA. And now, 1405. Each time, an external shock lit the fuse. But what kept the fire burning was the budget deficit, plugged with central bank money. That's why our average inflation over nearly ninety years has been above 17 percent. War and sanctions aren't ours to choose. But whether the orange bar stays lit for two years or ten — that's our choice. @sadegh_alhosseini

The seven-day average of oil flowing out of Hormuz has reached about 13.5 million barrels per day — nearly back to its peak during the Iran-US memorandum of understanding period, in Tir. Before the war it was around 20 million, and in Esfand it suddenly dropped below 2 million. But Iran's share of this flow is almost zero. Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, and Kuwait are filling the gap.
